claim: SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in late 2019 and is the causative agent of the ongoing coronavirus pandemic.
source: SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in late 2019 and is the causative agent of the ongoing coronavirus pandemic (Chang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2020

claim: The emergence of numerous variants of concern has created an additional challenge to treatment and prevention efforts.
source: However, the emergence of numerous variants of concern has created an additional challenge to treatment and prevention efforts.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 variants and their impact on public health

claim: The periodic emergence of new variants of concern beginning with Alpha, and later including Delta and most recently Omicron BA.1, have contributed to surges in cases worldwide.
source: The periodic emergence of new variants of concern beginning with Alpha, and later including Delta and most recently Omicron BA.1, have contributed to surges in cases worldwide (Wassenaar et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wassenaar et al., 2022

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is a member of the family Coronavirdae along with other human pathogens including SARS-CoV and MERS.
source: SARS-CoV-2 is a member of the family Coronavirdae along with other human pathogens including SARS-CoV and MERS (Corman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corman et al., 2018

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 virion is enveloped and encapsulates a 30 kb +ssRNA genome that encodes envelope (E) protein, membrane (M) protein, spike (S) protein, as well as 16 non-structural proteins and nine accessory proteins.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 virion is enveloped and encapsulates a 30 kb +ssRNA genome that encodes envelope (E) protein, membrane (M) protein, spike (S) protein, as well as 16 non-structural proteins and nine accessory proteins (Ke et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ke et al., 2020

claim: S is a critical viral protein for SARS-CoV-2 entry that is targeted by neutralizing antibodies and plays a multifunctional role in the infection process.
source: S, a critical viral protein for SARS-CoV-2 entry that is targeted by neutralizing antibodies, plays a multifunctional role in the infection process and is, therefore, a target for vaccine development (Martínez-Flores et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martínez-Flores et al., 2021

claim: S is a glycosylated homotrimer with each monomer consisting of S1 and S2 subunits.
source: S is a glycosylated homotrimer with each monomer consisting of S1 and S2 subunits (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and B showing the structure

claim: The S1 domain comprises an N-terminal domain (NTD), a receptor-binding domain (RBD), and two subdomains SD1 and 2, with the RBD mediating the interaction interface with the human ACE2 receptor.
source: The S1 domain comprises an N-terminal domain (NTD), a receptor-binding domain (RBD), and two subdomains SD1 and 2, with the RBD mediating the interaction interface with the human ACE2 receptor (Lan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lan et al., 2020

claim: The S2 domain includes the S1/S2 and S2 proteolytic cleavage sites as well as a fusion peptide.
source: The S2 domain includes the S1/S2 and S2 proteolytic cleavage sites as well as a fusion peptide.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of spike protein structure

claim: S plays three critical roles in facilitating host cell entry: S must bind ACE2, be proteolytically processed, and promote membrane fusion.
source: S plays three critical roles in facilitating host cell entry: S must bind ACE2, be proteolytically processed, and promote membrane fusion.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of spike protein function

claim: During the viral entry process, the S is processed by furin protease at the S1/S2 cleavage site either prior to or after S binding to ACE2 receptor.
source: During the viral entry process, the S is processed by furin protease at the S1/S2 cleavage site either prior to or after S binding to ACE2 receptor.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of spike protein processing

claim: Secondary cleavage by a separate protease (commonly transmembrane serine protease 2 (TMPRSS2) or cathepsin) at the S2 site leads to dissociation of S1 and release of the S2 subunit to drive membrane fusion and cellular entry.
source: This enables secondary cleavage by a separate protease (commonly transmembrane serine protease 2 (TMPRSS2) or cathepsin) at the S2 site (Peacock et al., 2021; Shang et al., 2020; Vankadari, 2020), which leads to dissociation of S1 and release of the S2 subunit to drive membrane fusion and cellular entry.
evidence: Supported by citations to Peacock et al., 2021; Shang et al., 2020; Vankadari, 2020

claim: Altered conformations in mutant S from variants would impact interactions of S with ACE2 and downstream functions.
source: Altered conformations in mutant S from variants would impact interactions of S with ACE2 (Raghuvamsi et al., 2021) and downstream functions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Raghuvamsi et al., 2021 and logical inference

claim: S is a hotspot for mutations in emerging variants.
source: Due to its key roles in viral host recognition and entry, it is unsurprising that S is a hotspot for mutations in emerging variants (Tian et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tian et al., 2021

claim: D614G emerged as a dominant mutation in 2020.
source: Among the first set of mutations that were detected in S variants during the early phase of the pandemic, D614G emerged as a dominant mutation in 2020 (Chang et al., 2020; Pandey et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang et al., 2020; Pandey et al., 2021

claim: A comparison of wild-type (WT) and D614G S revealed a ~50 X enhancement in proteolytic processing by furin.
source: One of the striking effects observed in a comparison of wild-type (WT) and D614G S revealed a~50 X enhancement in proteolytic processing by furin (Gobeil et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gobeil et al., 2021

claim: The Alpha variant emerged in September 2020 and includes mutations in addition to D614G localized to NTD, RBD, the furin-binding site, and the S2 subunit.
source: The Alpha variant subsequently emerged in September 2020, and in addition to D614G, other mutations localized to NTD (del 69–70, del 144), RBD (N501Y, A570D), the furin-binding site (P681H), and the S2 subunit (T716I, S982A, and D1118H) (Xia et al., 2021; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xia et al., 2021 and reference to Figure 1C and D

claim: The Delta variant was first identified in October 2020 and replaced the Alpha variant.
source: A more dominant Delta variant, first identified in October 2020 replaced the Alpha variant.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of variant emergence timeline

claim: The Delta variant S includes mutations in the NTD, RBD, furin cleavage site, and the S2 subunit.
source: The Delta variant S included mutations in the NTD (T19R, G142D, del 156–157, R158G), RBD (L452R, T478K), furin cleavage site (P681R), and the S2 subunit (D950N) (Tian et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tian et al., 2021

claim: The Omicron variant (BA.1) was first identified in November 2021 and is the variant with the largest number of mutations relative to WT.
source: A more recent surge in infection has been due to the dominant Omicron variant (BA.1) first identified in November 2021 and is the variant with the largest number of mutations relative to WT (Figure 1C and D; Liu et al., 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2022a and reference to Figure 1C and D

claim: The D614G mutation has been conserved across all major variants of concern.
source: Notably, the D614G mutation has been conserved across all major variants of concern (Wassenaar et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wassenaar et al., 2022

claim: The P681R mutation found in the Delta S and Omicron BA.1 S has been found to increase pathogenicity and proteolytic processing.
source: Additionally, the P681R mutation found in the Delta S and Omicron BA.1 S has been found to increase pathogenicity and proteolytic processing (Liu et al., 2022b; Saito et al., 2021), and RBD mutations in variants of concern have been found to increase affinity for the ACE2 receptor (Han et al., 2022; Ozono et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2022b; Saito et al., 2021

claim: RBD mutations in variants of concern have been found to increase affinity for the ACE2 receptor.
source: Additionally, the P681R mutation found in the Delta S and Omicron BA.1 S has been found to increase pathogenicity and proteolytic processing (Liu et al., 2022b; Saito et al., 2021), and RBD mutations in variants of concern have been found to increase affinity for the ACE2 receptor (Han et al., 2022; Ozono et al., 2021).

claim: Omicron shows the highest affinity for ACE2 among preceding variants, attributable to several mutations on the RBD.

claim: Viral fitness in SARS-CoV-2 has been quantified by competition assays involving the co-infection of two variant strains in airway cell lines and animal models.
source: Viral fitness in SARS-CoV-2 has been quantified by competition assays involving the co-infection of two variant strains in airway cell lines and animal models.

claim: D614G S showed greater fitness than WT S.

evidence: Supported by citation to Plante et al., 2021

claim: Alpha S showed greater fitness than D614G S.
source: From these experiments, it was concluded that D614G S showed greater fitness than WT S (Plante et al., 2021), Alpha S showed greater fitness than D614G S (Ulrich et al., 2022), and Delta S showed greater fitness than Alpha S (Liu et al., 2022b), which likely contributed to new surges in human infections.

claim: Delta S showed greater fitness than Alpha S.

claim: Cryo-EM structures do not completely capture all of the interconverting conformations in solution.

source: Multiple conformations showing RBD in 'up' or 'down' orientations have been observed by cryo-EM.

claim: Comparative HDXMS analysis of recombinant WT, D614G, Alpha, Delta, and Omicron BA.1 S variants reveals that the timeline of emergence corresponds to an overall stabilizing effect on the S trimer, together with altered dynamics in the NTD and RBD.
source: Comparative HDXMS analysis of recombinant WT, D614G, Alpha, Delta, and Omicron BA.1 S variants has allowed us to track changes in intrinsic dynamics across conserved regions of S through the progressively emerging variants of concern. Our results reveal that the timeline of emergence corresponds to an overall stabilizing effect on the S trimer, together with altered dynamics in the NTD and RBD.
